job: Fresh graduate in computing and engineering
name: Aisha Schmidt

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I live with my parents and my two younger brothers in a busy house in Calder Vale, so I do my applications at the dining table before anyone wakes up. After breakfast I study for a security certificate, and in the afternoon I help my mother prepare food for the community centre's lunch club. I finished computer science with a cybersecurity focus eight months ago, top of my class, and my final project was a tool to spot phishing emails for small charities. I interned at a bank's security team and at an IT support firm. I'm engaged to Yusuf, who's an electrician, and we'd planned a wedding for next autumn, but I'm not sure we can afford it without my salary.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it to other graduates, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's what my father said all along: new things are overpromised. I'd tell friends that careful, honest work will still matter. I'd say it at the community centre rather than online, because I'm not one for arguing on the internet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it means a normal job market, which is a slow one. I've had 85 applications and seven interviews, and one final-round near miss at a bank. I have about two months saved and a loan, and the wedding deposit is sitting there. I don't think I'm behind, but I feel the calendar.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep applying, mostly to banks, councils and security firms. I'd finish my certificate in the next two months so my CV shows it. I'd also ask my cousin, who works at an insurance firm, to forward my CV. And I'd talk to Yusuf and our families about whether to keep the wedding date.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Patient on the outside, a bit knotted inside. Like when you hold a hot dish and smile because guests are watching.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you feel the calendar. What do you mean?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The wedding, mostly. We have a date and a hall booked. If I don't have a job by spring, we either shrink the wedding or delay it, and both feel like failing. No sensible person would say so.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who has helped you most with the job search?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My mother's friend Mrs Rahman, who sits on a school board and knows a manager at the bank. She gave me an honest read of my interview answers. She said I downplay what I've built. I'm working on it.

say: I'd say careful, honest work will still matter, and the **hype** was overpromised.
I'd say it in person at the community centre, not **online**.
think: A normal job market is a **slow** one, and I feel the calendar with the wedding approaching.
I may be **downplaying** what I've built, as Mrs Rahman told me.
do: Finish the **security certificate** in the next two months.
Ask my cousin to forward my CV to the **insurance firm**.
Talk with Yusuf and our families about the **wedding date**.
feel: Patient outside, **knotted** inside, like holding a hot dish while smiling.
S0.quote: If I don't have a job by spring, we either shrink the wedding or delay it, and both feel like failing.
fieldNote: Aisha measures time by the **wedding** date and the hall deposit.
She says **no one** would blame her for delaying, but she feels it as failing.
Her network runs through **family and community** rather than online platforms.

steps.text: Finish the security certificate within two months
Apply to banks, councils and security firms every week
Ask my cousin to forward my CV to the insurance firm
Talk with Yusuf and both families about keeping the wedding date

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the second picture. It's called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it to other graduates, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it sounds like change we'll have to live through, and I'd tell friends to be steady and honest about it. I'd say firms should treat staff fairly, and not drop people just because software can do a part of the work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Cybersecurity is both a target and an opportunity. Writing code and checking logs is what AI will do first, but someone must defend against AI-made attacks. I think there'd be fewer junior jobs and more demand for people who understand risk and can explain it to a manager.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start using the tools for log analysis and report writing, so I can say I've done it. I'd aim at risk and compliance roles, which need judgement and trust. I'd also put some time into explaining security to small charities, since I made that phishing tool and many of them can't pay a firm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Concerned, but focused. It's like a change in the weather: you take a coat and keep walking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd start using the tools. What changed your mind?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I used one for my project and it helped with test data, but it made up an attack that doesn't exist. So I use it with care. If firms will test for it, I want to be able to say I can use it and also catch its mistakes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you explain this to your parents?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them this. The work changes shape, but it doesn't disappear for people who are careful. My father would nod and then ask about my savings. He worries in a quiet way, so I'd show him a monthly plan.

say: I'd say firms should treat staff **fairly** and not drop people because software does part of the work.
I'd tell friends to be **steady and honest**.
think: Writing code and checking logs go first, but someone has to **defend** against AI-made attacks.
Risk and **compliance** roles need judgement and trust, so I'd aim there.
do: Use AI for **log analysis** and report writing, and say so in interviews.
Aim for **risk and compliance** roles that need judgement.
Offer to explain security to small **charities** that can't pay a firm.
feel: **Concerned but focused**, like taking a coat and carrying on in new weather.
S1.quote: The work changes shape, but it doesn't disappear for people who are careful.
fieldNote: Aisha uses AI with **care** after it invented a non-existent attack.
She links **trust and judgement** to the roles she would fit.
Her instinct to help **small charities** reflects community values.

steps.text: Use AI for log analysis and report drafts, then check every finding
Apply for risk and compliance roles at banks and insurers
Offer paid security checks to small charities near Calder Vale

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the third picture. It's called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it to other graduates, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years is very fast. I'd say we need families and communities to hold together, and the government to protect people who lose work. I'd say the church and community centre should start planning to help, because they'll be needed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think my degree loses a lot of value. If AI can do almost any thinking work, then security analysis is mostly done by machines. The robots come later, maybe 2031, so hands-on work buys time. Yusuf's electrician work is safe for longer than mine, and that matters.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take any steady job quickly, even support work, to build income. I'd put the wedding on a smaller plan, with a modest meal at the community hall. I'd cut spending, and I'd ask my parents if I can contribute to the household budget rather than hold back. And I'd learn some practical skills with Yusuf, like basic wiring.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightened, though I'd try to be calm for my brothers. They look to me for how to feel.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why would you simplify the wedding?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because starting a marriage in debt is the opposite of what we want, and a smaller wedding is still a wedding. My mother would be sad at first, then she'd get busy cooking for the whole street, and that would be lovely in its own way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you share this with Yusuf?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Directly. He'd say we're a team, and I'd believe him. I'd also say if the next two years are hard, I'm glad it's him I'm facing it with, and I'd mean it.

say: I'd say **families and communities** must hold together, and the government should protect people who lose work.
I'd ask the church and community centre to **plan** to help.
think: My degree loses a lot of **value** if machines do most thinking work.
Yusuf's **electrician** work is safe for longer than mine, and that matters.
do: Take any **steady job** quickly, even support work.
Shrink the wedding to a modest meal at the **community hall**.
Learn **basic wiring** with Yusuf as a hands-on skill.
feel: **Frightened**, but I'd stay calm for my brothers.
S2.quote: Starting a marriage in debt is the opposite of what we want, and a smaller wedding is still a wedding.
fieldNote: Aisha's **family** is both her support and her responsibility; her brothers watch her mood.
She trades wedding **size** for stability without bitterness.
She values **Yusuf's** trade as a safer base for the household.

steps.text: Take any steady support or helpdesk job within two months
Cut spending and give a monthly share to the household budget
Shrink the wedding to a modest meal at the community hall
Learn basic wiring with Yusuf on Saturdays

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the fourth picture. It's called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it to other graduates, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years gives us a chance to prepare, and I'd say let's do that. I'd tell friends to pick a trade or skill that's anchored to people. I'd say communities should start training and mentoring now, not wait for the government.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think five years lets me be someone useful in my field before it changes. If I get a risk-and-compliance job this year, I'd have four years of experience when AGI arrives. Trust and accountability can't be fully handed to a machine, or not as quickly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take the first security or compliance job, study for a professional exam and save for our wedding and a small home. I'd marry Yusuf next autumn if we can, in a simpler way. I'd use AI for routine work and keep the judgement calls myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hopeful, with one eye on the clock. Like baking: you can't rush it, and you shouldn't walk away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does keeping the judgement calls mean?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If a client asks should we pay this ransom or should we shut the system, someone needs to be accountable. I'd want to be the accountable person, not the one who clicks accept on a report a machine wrote.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What could make you change this plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the bank cuts its graduate programme, or if our families' finances take a hit. We help each other here. If my father's shop slows, I'd put my savings in for my brothers' school fees first.

say: I'd tell friends to pick a skill **anchored to people**, and say communities should start mentoring now.
I'd say not to **wait** for the government.
think: Five years lets me become useful before the field changes, with **four years** of experience at AGI.
Trust and **accountability** can't be handed to a machine as quickly.
do: Take the first **security or compliance job** and study for a professional exam.
Marry **Yusuf** next autumn in a simpler way if we can.
Use AI for **routine work** and keep the judgement calls.
feel: **Hopeful**, with an eye on the clock, like baking you can't rush.
S3.quote: I'd want to be the accountable person, not the one who clicks accept on a report a machine wrote.
fieldNote: Aisha wants to be the **accountable** person, not the one who clicks accept.
Family finances come first: she'd fund her **brothers' school fees** if needed.
Wedding plans become the measure of a **normal life**.

steps.text: Take the first security or compliance job offered
Study for a professional security exam in the evenings
Use AI for routine reports and keep the judgement calls myself
Marry Yusuf next autumn in a simpler ceremony

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the fifth picture. It's called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it to other graduates, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years is long, and I'd say it should be used well. I'd tell friends to build their lives, not just their careers: marry, have children if they want, keep their faith and neighbours close. Online I'd say nothing, but at the centre I'd say it often.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be fine, I believe. A decade gives time to get a good job, build experience and pay off the loan. I'd also have children by then, God willing. What I'd worry about is my brothers, who are fifteen and thirteen, and what jobs they'll find.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take a job in the next six months, marry Yusuf next autumn and save for a flat. I'd study part-time for a professional qualification and mentor young women in tech through the community centre. I'd also help my brothers pick subjects that stay useful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Peaceful, and grateful. I know I'm lucky to have people around me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you teach your brothers?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: To understand how things work, not just how to click. And to be kind and reliable, because trust is going to be worth more than a certificate. I'd also tell them to learn a trade alongside school.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would be the hardest part?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Waiting for the first job. A long runway doesn't help someone who's wondering what to tell the bank about the wedding. After that, I think I'd be steady.

say: I'd tell friends to build their **lives**, not just careers, and keep neighbours close.
I'd say it at the **community centre**, not online.
think: A decade gives time for a good job, experience and **paying the loan**.
I worry most about my **brothers**, aged fifteen and thirteen.
do: Take a job in six months and marry **Yusuf** next autumn.
Study part time for a professional **qualification**.
Mentor young women in tech through the **community centre**.
feel: **Peaceful and grateful**, aware of how many people I have around me.
S4.quote: A long runway doesn't help someone who's wondering what to tell the bank about the wedding.
fieldNote: Aisha's calm is built on **people**: Yusuf, parents, community.
She wants her brothers to learn **how things work**, plus a trade.
The hardest part remains the **first job**.

steps.text: Take a security job within six months
Marry Yusuf next autumn and start saving for a flat
Study part time for a professional security qualification
Mentor young women in tech through the community centre

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. That's when a marriage, a family and a job all need to be settled, and the world is moving on top of them. What would help is a clear plan from government, communities that mentor, and employers who still take on graduates.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that I'm not a worrier by nature, but I carry a lot for people around me. If I can get the first job, I think I can carry the rest. I'd like to be given the chance to be useful.

headlineQuote: I'm not a worrier by nature, but I carry a lot for people around me.
portrait: Aisha is a 23-year-old **computer science** graduate with a cybersecurity focus, top of her class, living with her parents and two brothers.
She has had 85 applications and seven interviews, with two months of savings, a loan and a **wedding** deposit.
She is traditional and community-minded, favours work and family support over handouts, and is engaged to **Yusuf**, an electrician.
She uses AI with care, after it invented an attack, and aims at **risk and compliance** roles that need judgement.
Her mood follows the wedding calendar and her brothers' view of her, and **spikes** at two years.
biggestWorry: The two-year **AGI** picture worries her most because marriage, family and work would all need settling at once.
whatWouldHelp: She wants a clear **government plan**, community mentoring and employers who keep taking on graduates.
